The remanent magnetization of the rock is stable and it appears to be primary after a conglomerate test. Therefore no deformation structures postdating the acquisition of remanent magnetization can be inferred from palaeomagnetic data. Starkey and Palmer (1970) have pointed out that a small partial overprint superimposed along a consistent direction upon a random scatter of predepo- sitional remanence directions in conglomerate clasts is not readily detected by the randomness test. However, a partial overprint should result in systematic directional swings as individual conglomerate clasts are demagnetized since block- ing temperature spectra for the two magnetizations are unlikely to be identical (especially in clasts containing both magnetite and hematite, as at site 18). Also, a partial overprint should cause asymmetry in the reversal pattern observed between stably magnetized sites. A partial overprint in rocks of the Wigwam Formation seems unlikely because almost all speci- mens at sites 18 and 35 carry stable directions of magnetiza- tion, and mean directions for sites magnetized to the north and south are antiparallel within the limits of statistical uncer- tainty. Paleomagnetic investigations of the Emsian quartz sandstones from Holy Cross Mountains (Central Poland) have revealed the presence of a three-component natural remanent magnetization. The viscous component of the NRM is carried by magnetite grains and is directed close to the present-day local geomagnetic field. The remaining two components are both carried by hematite, presumably of two-stage origin. Because it was not possible to apply a fold test, the acquisition time of each component could only be inferred indirectly. The hematite remanence of the highest (65OOC) blocking temperature is thought to be of post-tectonic (Permian) origin, as its direction before bedding correction (D = 199 ‘, Z = - 38” ) is almost identical with the characteristic NRM obtained (Lewandowski, 1983) from neighbouring Permian deposits. The intermediate component (D = 231°, Z = 0, with a blocking temperature of around 610°C), after applying a bedding correction, gives a paleomagnetic pole (h = 24ON, S$ = 142OE) near to European Middle-Upper Devonian poles. Therefore, it is thought that this magnetization probably reflects the ambient geomagnetic field not very long after sedimentation. Introduction During the past few years, intensive pale

Paleomagnetic investigations of the Emsian quartz sandstones from Holy Cross Mountains (Central Poland) have revealed the presence of a three-component natural remanent magnetization. The viscous component of the NRM is carried by magnetite grains and is directed close to the present-day local geomagnetic field. The remaining two components are both carried by hematite, presumably of two-stage origin. Because it was not possible to apply a fold test, the acquisition time of each component could only be inferred indirectly. The hematite remanence of the highest (65OOC) blocking temperature is thought to be of post-tectonic (Permian) origin, as its direction before bedding correction (D = 199 ‘, Z = - 38” ) is almost identical with the characteristic NRM obtained (Lewandowski, 1983) from neighbouring Permian deposits. The intermediate component (D = 231°, Z = 0, with a blocking temperature of around 610°C), after applying a bedding correction, gives a paleomagnetic pole (h = 24ON, S$ = 142OE) near to European Middle-Upper Devonian poles. Therefore, it is thought that this magnetization probably reflects the ambient geomagnetic field not very long after sedimentation. Introducti

Introduction During the past few years, intensive paleo- magnetic studies of the Devonian rocks have been made both from the European continent (Abra- hamsen, 1977; Duff, 1980; Bachtadse et al., 1983; Perroud and Bonhommet, 1984) and the British Isles (Storetvedt and Carmichael, 1979; Storetvedt and Torsvik, 1983; Torsvik et al., 1983; Torsvik, 1984, 1985). Although unequivocal geotectonic in- terpretation of the results obtained so far is not possible, nonetheless some general conclusions have been drawn concerning geodynamic processes during the assembly of Pangea (e.g. Van der Voo, 1983). This paper reports paleomagnetic results from the Holy Cross Mountains (Central Poland). The investigation is part of the research program on the Upper Palaeozoic rocks from Norway (in- cluding Spitsbergen) and Poland, carried out by paleomagnetic groups in Bergen and Sogndal (Norway) and Warsaw (Poland). The Spitsbergen results have already been published (Lovlie et al., 1984; Jelehska and Lewandowski, in press). w poorly dated palaeomagnetic directions are reported from Africa, the other large plate inferred to have played an important role in the tectonic development of the Mediterranean region. In contrast to the major plates, the main sources of palaeomagnetic data in the Mediterranean have been Mesozoic and Palaeogene carbonates, precluding direct compari- son between directions measured from the Medi- terranean and the European and African plates. Thus, for a lack of a better solution, Mediter- ranean palaeopoles are usually compared with poles for Africa or Europe with the help of a plate tectonic reconstruction (VandenBerg, 1979, Lowrie et al., 1980, Marton and Marton, 1981, 1983). This procedure allows common trends or large relative movements in the Mediterranean to be recognized with respect to the major plates. However, there are shortcomings to the use of the “pseudo” ap- parent polar wander path (APWP) and work con- tinues to be directed in the stable areas at develop- ing better defined APWPs. Until additional results are reported from the stable areas, studies in structurally rotated terranes are best continued in strata the directions of which can be directly com- pared with those already reported from the major plates. Thus, for a lack of a better solution, Mediter- ranean palaeopoles are usually compared with poles for Africa or Europe with the help of a plate tectonic reconstruction (VandenBerg, 1979, Lowrie et al., 1980, Marton and Marton, 1981, 1983). This procedure allows common trends or large relative movements in the Mediterranean to be recognized with respect to the major plates. However, there are shortcomings to the use of the “pseudo” ap- parent polar wander path (APWP) and work con- tinues to be directed in the stable areas at develop- ing better defined APWPs. Until additional results are reported from the stable areas, studies in structurally rotated terranes are best continued in strata the directions of which can be directly com- pared with those already reported from the major plates. Because a Permian direction is one of these, we decided to renew our attack on the problem of obtaining reliable directions from the Hungarian red beds. Discussion The complex NRM at locality 6 (Table 1) serves as a base for evaluating the timing of acquisition of the remanence of red beds from the Balaton Highlands. The component 6a direction is consid- ered to be a primary remanence, although not necessarily of depositional origin for several rea- sons. It resides in haematite that is extremely resistant to thermal cleaning; the structurally un- corrected direction differs significantly from the present field direction, and the tilt-corrected in- clination is low enough to be a Permian inclina- tion. Additionally, the polarity may be concluded to be reverse by correlation with the already proven post-Permian counterclockwise rotation of the Transdanubian Central Mountains (e.g. Marton and Marton, 1983). Lastly, the declination after tilt correction agrees with some other directions interpreted as Permian from the eastern part of the Southern and Eastern Alps and the Inner West Carpathians (Fig. 7). 49 The overprint component at locality 6 (Table 1, direction 6b), although resistant to heating and differing significantly from the present field direc- tion, is less resistant to thermal cleaning than direction 6a. It shows a remarkable similarity to di

ions, and agreement of the struc- turally uncorrected ChRM direction of locality 1 with the secondary directions may be a coinci- dence. In any case, a general interpretation of palaeo- magnetic results from the Balaton Highlands in terms of tectonics is basically independent of the correct answer to the above question. With respect to stable Europe, represented by the Bohemian Massif in the present vicinity of the Pannonian Basin, a large counterclockwise rotation of the Balaton Highlands is evident. The amount of rota- tion exceeds 90” for the direction interpreted as Permian, and appears distinctly less for the over- printed normal polarity directions. The age of the first acquisition of an overprint magnetization car- ried by maghemite may be estimated as mid- Cretaceous on palaeomagnetic grounds (Fig. 8) i.e. it ties up with the geologically recognized uplift of the Transdanubian Central Mountains. The Permian rocks from the Mecsek Mountains yielded palaeomagnetic directions that are close to the Permian direction for stable Europe, although slightly but distinctly rotated counterclockwise rel- ative to it. For the Balaton Highlands, the component 1 direction agrees with directions obtained from Permian red beds and volcanics in the eastern part of the Southern and Eastern Alps and the Inner West Carpathians. The component 6a direction is consid- ered to be a primary remanence, although not necessarily of depositional origin for several rea- sons. Additionally, the polarity may be concluded to be reverse by correlation with the already proven post-Permian counterclockwise rotation of the Transdanubian Central Mountains (e.g. Marton and Marton, 1983). Lastly, the declination after tilt correction agrees with some other directions interpreted as Permian from the eastern part of the Southern and Eastern Alps and the Inner West Carpathians (Fig. 7). 49 The overprint component at locality 6 (Table 1, direction 6b), although resistant to heating and differing significantly from the present field direc- tion, is less resistant to thermal cleaning than direction 6a. Palaeomagnetic studies were carried out in Permian red beds of the Balaton Highlands, the Mecsek Mountains, and the Btkk Mountains of Hungary. Statistically well defined directions were obtained from six localities in the Balaton Highlands and two localities in the Mecsek Mountains. No meaningful results were obtained from the Blikk Mountains. Three magnetic components were identified from red beds of the Balaton Highlands: (1) in haematite with a very high unblocking temperature (7OOO C), interpreted as a Permian magnetization (0, = 79 ‘, Z, = - ll’, k = 24, as5 = 13.6 “), in six samples from three beds in a single locality; (2) a secondary but ancient component residing mainly inmaghemite(D=314O, I=49O, k=48, agS= 10.0 “), in 84 samples from six localities with a within-locality scatter increasing on unfolding; and (3) a direction parallel to the present field (D = 7 O, 1=62O, k=46,a9s=7.70),innine samples from a single locality. For the Balaton Highlands, the component 1 direction agrees with directions obtained from Permian red beds and volcanics in the eastern part of the Southern and Eastern Alps and the Inner West Carpathians. All show large, apparent rotations relative to stable Europe since the Permian. Compone

otations relative to stable Europe since the Permian. Component 2 is of post-folding (post-Aptian) age. Its direction agrees with known Late Cretaceous directions from the Transdanubian Central Mountains, which also show significant counterclockwise rotation relative to stable Europe. The characteristic magnetization for the Mecsek Mountains resides in haematite and may be primary. The directions indicate only a slight net counterclockwise rotation of the Mecsek Mountains with respect to stable Europe since the Permian. Paleomagnetic data for the middle-late Jurassic sediments from nine localities of Krakow-Czestochowa Upland belonging to stable Europe, and from three valleys of the Lower Subtatric Nappe belonging to mobile Europe are presented. The displacement is associ- ated with the late Cretaceous sub-Hercynian movements during the final stage of collision of the African and Eurasian plates (Kgdzialko- Hofmokl et al., 1985). The deposits sampled were nodular limestones and red and green radiolarites. They ranged in age from the Bathonian to the Kimmeridgian. The sedimentation rate of these rocks was rather slow, about 1.5 cm/lo4 years. The total amount of iron compounds (as Fe,O,) in radiolarites averages from 0.63 to 0.79wt.s. The petrographic proper- ties of the radiolarites suggest that the iron con- tained is of primary origin (Lefeld, 1974, Kadziatlro-Hofmokl et al., 1985). The tectonic en- vironment was more complicated than in the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland and structural cor- rections were more important. At exposure F the sampled radiolarites formed an overturned fold. Seventy-seven hand samples were collected from three sections, out of which slices and then 340 specimens were cut in the form of cubes and subjected to paleomagnetic investigations. de and, for few samples, acquisition and decay curves of IRM were measured. The thermomagnetic analy- sis was conducted with a spinner magnetometer equipped with a nonmagnetic oven installed inside a pickup coil. Three permalloy screens ensured cancellation of the external magnetic field. The maximum temperature reached in this apparatus is 700 ‘C, the temperature rises linearly at a rate 20 “-30 o C/mm. The experiments involved ther- mal demagnetization of isothermal remanence (J,,) acquired in 1.8 T during heating in the air to 600°C (the isothermal remanence is denoted J,, because in most cases it is a saturation remanence). Thermomagnetic curves (J,, vs. T) are plotted automatically by an XY recorder. From these curves, blocking temperatures ( Tb) characterizing magnetic minerals were obtained. Curves obtained during the second heating show the com- position of magnetic minerals in samples after heating in the air. The mean direction obtained for K3 differs in declination by about 180” from the mean direction of the ChRM of normal polarity for the late Callovian stromatolites from K2 (see Fig. 6 and Table 2). The results of the a.f. demagnetization experi- ments for CZ specimens show that the NRM is a resultant of the low- and high-coercivity compo- nents of different directions. The high-coercivity component is probably connected with goethite. Paleomagnetic data for the middle-late Jurassic sediments from nine localities of Krakow-Czestochowa Upland belonging to stable Europe, and from three valleys of the Lower Subtatric Nappe belonging to mobile Europe are presented. The majority of the rocks investigated comprising limestones, stromatolites and radiolarites were found to be normally magnetized. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) of reversed polarity were found in limestones and stromatolites of middle Callovian age from the stable region and in one exposure of Oxfordian radiolarites from the mobile region. Along one of the middle Callovian sections studied the NRM direction of the specimens changed from R to N. The mean paleomagnetic pole positions obtained for the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland (lat. 72.3ON, long. 150.4O E, as5 = 7.3”) and for the Lower Subtatric Nappe (lat. 71.7 N, long. 132.2O E, as5 = 4.3O) are consistent with the data for stable Europe

ormally magnetized. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) of reversed polarity were found in limestones and stromatolites of middle Callovian age from the stable region and in one exposure of Oxfordian radiolarites from the mobile region. Along one of the middle Callovian sections studied the NRM direction of the specimens changed from R to N. The mean paleomagnetic pole positions obtained for the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland (lat. 72.3ON, long. 150.4O E, as5 = 7.3”) and for the Lower Subtatric Nappe (lat. 71.7 N, long. 132.2O E, as5 = 4.3O) are consistent with the data for stable Europe (lat. 74.7 O N, long. 147.1O E, ass = 5.0 o ). The paleomagnetic results presented do not reveal any major relative rotations either within the Lower Subtatric Nappe or between this area and the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland. The reversed directions of NRM observed indicate the existence of a period of reversed field direction in the Middle Callovian and perhaps also in the Oxfordian. Introduction In Poland Jurassic deposits are found in two distinct tectonic units here referred to as stable Europe and mobile Europe. The stable plate com- prises all of Europe north of the Carpathian block and extends longitudinally from the Caucasus to the Pyrenees. Mobile Europe is the series of smaller plates which lay b

Poland. It embraces the Polish Carpathian region with the Tatra Moun- tains and the Pieniny Klippen belt. The suture zone of the African and Eurasian plates is prob- ably located slightly north of the Pieniny Klippen Belt, under the Carpathian flysch layer. Figure 1A shows the location of Jurassic sediments in Po- land. The main purpose of this study was to de- termine the mean paleomagnetic poles for mid- dle-late Jurassic time for that part of Poland which belongs to stable Europe, e.g., the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland. Hitherto the only reliable paleomagnetic data for the Jurassic for 54 stable Europe was that determined from samples from southern Germany (Heller, 1977, 1978), En- gland (Hijab and Tarling, 1982), the French-Swiss Jura (Johnson et al., 1984), and the Russian Plat- form (Khramov, 1984). In addition, paleomagnetic studies of sediments from the Lower Subtatric Nappe in the Carpathians (2 in Fig. 1A) were undertaken in order to find out (a) whether this mobile region had moved relative to stable Europe, and (b) whether movements within this region itself could be detected. Further studies of the sediments from the region of the Pieniny Klippen Belt (3 in Fig. 1A) and Kujawy (4 in the same Figure) are cur- rently in progress. In this paper we p

In this paper we present the results obtained for the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland from the following exposures (Fig. 1B): Wielun- W; Lisowice-LI; Ogrodzieniec-OG; Klobuck- KI, K2, K3; Stare Gliny-SGI, SG2; Zalas-Z; Podleze-POI, PO2 (stromatolites) and PW (limestones); Czatkowice-CZ. Preliminary re- sults have already been reported (Kruczyk et al., 1980; Kruczyk and Kadzialko-Hofmokl, 1983). Results from three exposures from the Tatra Mountains: Chochdowska Valley-CH; Lejowa Valley-L; Filipka Valley--F, shown in Fig. lC, have already been published (Kqdzialko-Hofmokl et al., 1985). Preliminary results from samples of Jurassic deposits from the Balkan region in Bulgaria (Kruczyk et al., 1986) have also been included in the summarizing table. Paleomagnetic data for the middle-late Jurassic sediments from nine localities of Krakow-Czestochowa Upland belonging to stable Europe, and from three valleys of the Lower Subtatric Nappe belonging to mobile Europe are presented. The majority of the rocks investigated comprising limestones, stromatolites and radiolarites were found to be normally magnetized. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) of reversed polarity were found in limestones and stromatolites of middle Callovian age from the stable region and in one exposure of Oxfordian radiolarites from the mobile region. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) of reversed polarity were found in limestones and stromatolites of middle Callovian age from the stable region and in one exposure of Oxfordian radiolarites from the mobile region. Along one of the middle Callovian sections studied the NRM direction of the specimens changed from R to N. The mean paleomagnetic pole positions obtained for the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland (lat. 72.3ON, long. 150.4O E, as5 = 7.3”) and for the Lower Subtatric Nappe (lat. 71.7 N, long. 132.2O E, as5 = 4.3O) are consistent with the data for stable Europe (lat. 74.7 O N, long. 147.1O E, ass = 5.0 o ). The paleomagnetic results presented do not reveal any major relative rotations either within the Lower Subtatric Nappe or between this area and the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland. The reversed directions of NRM observed indicate the existence of a period of reversed field direction in the Middle Callovian and perhaps also in the Oxfordian. Introduction In Poland Jurassic deposits are found in two distinct tectonic units here referred to as stable Europe and mobile Europe. The stable plate com- prises all of Europe north of the Carpathian block and extends longitudinally from the Caucasus to the Pyrenees. Mobile Europe is the series of smaller plates which lay b

Poland. It embraces the Polish Carpathian region with the Tatra Moun- tains and the Pieniny Klippen belt. The suture zone of the African and Eurasian plates is prob- ably located slightly north of the Pieniny Klippen Belt, under the Carpathian flysch layer. Figure 1A shows the location of Jurassic sediments in Po- land. The main purpose of this study was to de- termine the mean paleomagnetic poles for mid- dle-late Jurassic time for that part of Poland which belongs to stable Europe, e.g., the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland. Hitherto the only reliable paleomagnetic data for the Jurassic for 54 stable Europe was that determined from samples from southern Germany (Heller, 1977, 1978), En- gland (Hijab and Tarling, 1982), the French-Swiss Jura (Johnson et al., 1984), and the Russian Plat- form (Khramov, 1984). In addition, paleomagnetic studies of sediments from the Lower Subtatric Nappe in the Carpathians (2 in Fig. 1A) were undertaken in order to find out (a) whether this mobile region had moved relative to stable Europe, and (b) whether movements within this region itself could be detected. In this paper we present the results obtained for the Krakow-Czestochowa Upland from the following exposures (Fig. 1B): Wielun- W; Lisowice-LI; Ogrodzieniec-OG; Klobuck- KI, K2, K3; Stare Gliny-SGI, SG2; Zalas-Z; Podleze-POI, PO2 (stromatolites) and PW (limestones); Czatkowice-CZ. Preliminary re- sults have already been reported (Kruczyk et al., 1980; Kruczyk and Kadzialko-Hofmokl, 1983). Results from three exposures from the Tatra Mountains: Chochdowska Valley-CH; Lejowa Valley-L; Filipka Valley--F, shown in Fig. lC, have already been published (Kqdzialko-Hofmokl et al., 1985). Preliminary results from samples of Jurassic deposits from the Balkan region in Bulgaria (Kruczyk et al., 1986) have also been included in the summarizing table. The marine platform carbonates and elastics range in age from early Cambrian to early Triassic. Progressive alternating field and/or thermal demagnetization analyses reveal predomi- nantly single component magnetizations, sometimes of both normal and reverse polarity. Laboratory tests for palaeomagnetic stability Pilot samples were selected from each locality and subjected to laboratory tests for stability using an alternating field up to an maximum amplitude of 140 mT and by heating in a magnetically com- pensated medium (Km, 1969). In the course of alternating field demagnetiza- tion the specimen was rotated at a ratio of angular velocities of 5 : 4, each specimen being placed in the demagnetization coils in two mutually per- pendicular positions. In the thermal demagnetiza- tion experiments, the specimens were heated in a non-magnetic furnace to the Curie point of haematite. The compensation of the magnetic field in the Helmholtz coils was controlled by the MAVACS system (designed by J. Halousek, B. PeSina and K. Pfihoda) which guarantees auto- matic compensation to within 2 nT. The studied rocks were measured using highly sensitive spinner magnetometers of the JR-4 type (Jelinek, 1966). Each heating cycle was followed by a determina- tion of the mean magnetic susceptibility in order to record any mineral phase changes which may have occurred in the rock. Groups of normally and reversely polarized andesite tuffs were found even within a single outcrop by means of thermal field demagnetization and multicomponent analysis of the magnetization. With a view to the number of samples (177) suitable for analysis and the number of localities (9), the reported palaeomagnetic data should be considered as preliminary. The interpreted results indicate a different palaeogeographic evolution of northern and southern Mongolia relative to the Siberian platform and North China in the Permian and Carboniferous. On the other hand, similar apparent polar wander paths for North China (Lin et al., 1985) and the studied regions of northern and southern Mongolia indicate similar palaeogeographic evolution in the Permian to Carboniferous. Introduction The palaeogeographic evolution of Mongolia during the upper Palaeozoic and Mesozoic is a very important problem, particularly with respect to its relationship with the Siberian platform to the north and the North China block to the south. Laboratory tests for palaeomagnetic stability Pilot samples were selected from each locality and subjected to laboratory tests for stability using an alternating field up to an maximum amplitude of 140 mT and by heating in a magnetically com- pensated medium (Km, 1969). In the course of alternating field demagnetiza- tion the specimen was rotated at a ratio of angular velocities of 5 : 4, each specimen being placed in the demagnetization coils in two mutually per- pendicular positions. In the thermal demagnetiza- tion experiments, the specimens were heated in a non-magnetic furnace to the Curie point of haematite. The compensation of the magnetic field in the Helmholtz coils was controlled by the MAVACS system (designed by J. Halousek, B. PeSina and K. Pfihoda) which guarantees auto- matic compensation to within 2 nT. The studied rocks were measured using highly sensitive spinner magnetometers of the JR-4 type (Jelinek, 1966). Each heating cycle was followed by a determina- tion of the mean magnetic susceptibility in order to record any mineral phase changes which may have occurred in the rock. Laboratory tests for palaeomagnetic stability Pilot samples were selected from each locality and subjected to laboratory tests for stability using an alternating field up to an maximum amplitude of 140 mT and by heating in a magnetically com- pensated medium (Km, 1969). In the course of alternating field demagnetiza- tion the specimen was rotated at a ratio of angular velocities of 5 : 4, each specimen being placed in the demagnetization coils in two mutually per- pendicular positions. In the thermal demagnetiza- tion experiments, the specimens were heated in a non-magnetic furnace to the Curie point of haematite. The compensation of the magnetic field in the Helmholtz coils was controlled by the MAVACS system (designed by J. Halousek, B. PeSina and K. Pfihoda) which guarantees auto- matic compensation to within 2 nT. The studied rocks were measured using highly sensitive spinner magnetometers of the JR-4 type (Jelinek, 1966). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Cantabric Chain and the Sierra de 10s Cameros (northern Spain) reveals that the N.R.M. contains four types of ~rn~n~ts tentatively classified in decreasing ages. The older components (group 1) are considered as the primary ma~e~tion. They yield a paleomagnetic pole located at lat. 41°N,long.237*E(n=6, k=186*, ass= 5 “). This pole position implies the existence of a large upper Jurassic-lower Cretaceous swing in the Iberian polar-wander path. The comparison with other polar paths (North America, Africa) supports the hypothesis of an initial lower Cretaceous rotation of Iberia prior to the main mid-Cretaceous shift. The remainder of the components represent remagnetizations. The major phase (groups 2 and 3) extended from the upper Cretaceous to the Eocene at least, a period closely correlated with the period of convergence between the European and Iberian plates. The directions of group 3 are characterized by low inclination. This is a common behaviour for Eocene directions in the Mediterranean area. Previous data obtained from the Wealden redbeds largely agrees with the directions of one or other of the groups 2 and 3. Introduction Recent developments in the kinematics of the Iberian plate have stressed the importance of the lower Cretaceous in its evolution. Therefore, it is of major importance to get paleomagnetic data for this period. The continental deposits known as the Wealden facies, outcropping in the Cantabrian Chain and in the Sierra de 10s Cameros at the ~orthweste~ end of the Iberian chain, offer a good opportunity for a paleomagnetic study. Pre- vious results obtained by Stauffer and Tarling (1971) from one site and Van den Berg (1979) from two sites were merely interpreted as antedat- ing the rotation of the Iberian Peninsula, contem- ~~-1951/87/$03.50 @ 1987 Ekevier Science Publishers B.V. poraneous with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. This assumption supposes (1) that the measured magnetic directions are of primary origin and (2) that the European paleomagnetic poles of similar age are fairly well defined. Unfortunately, the second condition is far from being realized as can be observed, for example, in a recent compilation made by Westphal et al. (1985). We will be dealing later on with the first condition. In order to increase the reliability of the lower Cretaceous Iberian paleomagnetic pole, we have carried out a more extensive study of the Wealden series, mainly in the Sierra de 10s Cameros, where the sedimentary basin is best developped and the formations well exposed. This proved to be a safe procedure in this study, which revealed that the magnetic history of the Wealden series is much more intricate than expected. The continental sediments deposited in the lower Cretaceous in northern Spain followed the Jurassic marine sedimentation. They are indicative of a distensive phase beginning in the Pyrenean and Cantabrian area in the upper Jurassk The sediments accumulated in two basins: the Cantabrian basin to the north and the Soria basin or Sierra de 10s Cameros to the south. In the other states of the Commonwealth, attempts by purely geological methods to extend the two-fold division established in Victoria have been successful to some extent, but in many cases it is impossible to define ages with any degree of certainty. The difference in direction between the Older and Newer Volcanics in Victoria should exist in basalts of earlier and later Cainozoic age elsewhere, so that palaeomagnetic data may be of assistance in stratigraphic correlation. From palaeomagnetic surveys of some rock formations in Australia the movements of the geomagnetic pole relative to Australia during and since the Upper Proterozoic has been obtained in broad outline. The data are very far from complete but sufficient is known for certain general points to be made. The path of movement is known in some detail from Carboniferous to Recent times and with less certainty for periods prior to this. The stability of the magnetization of several of the rock formations studied has been demonstrated (Irving 1956, 1957a) by tests of the type described by Graham (1949). During the late Silurian and early Devonian it was situated in a similar longitude but well south in the Southern Ocean. Because of the occurrence of reversals of magnetization the palaeomagnetic method, although it determines the position of the pole, does not give its polarity. The rock types include the Canberra Volcanics and Porphyries, the Murrumbidgee Sandstones and the Nethercote Basalts. Throughout these formations and irrespective of the rock type the directions of magnetization are remarkably uniform. The low inclination of the direction of remanent magnetization in

ustralia lay 10-1s' away from the equator, the pole lying in the South Atlantic. Evidence for stability of the rocks is as follows: (I) their uniformity of direction, (2) the deviation from the present geomagnetic and dipole fields, (3) the presence of normal and reversely magnetized rocks. These data lend support to the belief that south-eastern Australia experienced tropical conditions during the Devonian. Introduction Preliminary work by IRVING and GREEN (1958) indicated that between the Cambriam and Carboniferous Periods Australia moved from a low latitude to a high polar one. Furthermore, palaeomagnetic determinations on nine samples from the Mugga Porphyry (Upper Silurian) and on twelve samples from the Ainslie Volcanics (Upper Silurian and/or Lower Devonian) indicate a low latitude for the sampling area. This indication together with the high latitude of south-eastern Austra- lia as found by IRVING (1957) working on Upper Carboniferous varves suggested that large changes in the inclination of the geomag- netic field had taken place during the Devonian and/or Lower Carboniferous. MANWARING Department of Geophysics, Australian National University, Canberra Introduction In the area of the Sydney Basin there are a large number of basic igneous rock bodies whose ages are defined only within wide limits. They are intruded into or extruded upon the Triassic Hawkesbury and Wianamatta Groups. These rocks are thus either Upper- or post- Triassic in age, and have generally been con- sidered as Tertiary (David, 1950). A _ palaeo- magnetic study was made of three of these rock bodies (Fig. 1) with a view to obtaining a more precise estimate of their age. (1) A dyke of porphyritic olivine dolerite at Luddenham, N.S.W. (33° 53'S, 150° 40’ E ; map ref.: 703120, Liverpool 1-mile Military, No. 422, Zone 8). (2) An intrusive (? laccolith) of fine grained Olivine dolerite at Peat’s Ridge, N.S.W. Soe 19 5, 1bl° 12’ EE; map ref.: 217805, Gosford & Norahville 1-mile Military, Nos. 410 & 411, Zone 8). (3) The basalt flow or flows capping Mt. Tomah in the Blue Mountains of N.S.W. (83° 32'S, 150° 26’E; map ref.: 415550, Katoomba 1-mile Military, No. 415, Zone 8). . This study was begun as part of an Honours thesis in the Department of Geology and Geophysics at the University of Sydney, and completed in the Departme

te at Peat’s Ridge, N.S.W. Soe 19 5, 1bl° 12’ EE; map ref.: 217805, Gosford & Norahville 1-mile Military, Nos. 410 & 411, Zone 8). (3) The basalt flow or flows capping Mt. Tomah in the Blue Mountains of N.S.W. (83° 32'S, 150° 26’E; map ref.: 415550, Katoomba 1-mile Military, No. 415, Zone 8). . This study was begun as part of an Honours thesis in the Department of Geology and Geophysics at the University of Sydney, and completed in the Department of Geophysics, Australian National University, Canberra. I wish to thank Dr. A. A. Day at Sydney, and Mr. E. Irving at Canberra, for much help and advice on this work. Methods Employed In each case, samples were distributed as evenly as possible over the total exposures of rock available. At Luddenham, exposure is restricted to three small excavations made some years ago when the rock was quarried as road metal for a short time. Seven oriented samples were taken along about 50 yards of the dyke. At Peat’s Ridge, five oriented samples were taken from different places on the working face of the road metal quarry in operation there. On Mt. Tomah, six oriented samples were taken from cuttings on a road (Bell’s Line of Road) which crosses the basalt outcrop. Methods Employed In each case, samples were distributed as evenly as possible over the total exposures of rock available. At Luddenham, exposure is restricted to three small excavations made some years ago when the rock was quarried as road metal for a short time. Seven oriented samples were taken along about 50 yards of the dyke. At Peat’s Ridge, five oriented samples were taken from different places on the working face of the road metal quarry in operation there. On Mt. Tomah, six oriented samples were taken from cuttings on a road (Bell’s Line of Road) which crosses the basalt outcrop. Between one and three cylindrical specimens (14 inches in diameter ; between 4 and 13 inches in height) were cut from each oriented sample. The intensities and directions of the natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of the specimens were measured firstly on the astatic magnetometer in the Department of Geology and Geophysics, Sydney Uni

here. On Mt. Tomah, six oriented samples were taken from cuttings on a road (Bell’s Line of Road) which crosses the basalt outcrop. Between one and three cylindrical specimens (14 inches in diameter ; between 4 and 13 inches in height) were cut from each oriented sample. The intensities and directions of the natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of the specimens were measured firstly on the astatic magnetometer in the Department of Geology and Geophysics, Sydney University, in 1960, and later on an astatic magnetometer in the Department of Geophysics, Australian National University, in 1961-62. The stability of the specimens was studied by demagnetization in alternating magnetic fields (Thellier and Rimbert, 1954 and 1955), using the apparatus and procedures described by Irving, Stott and Fic. l Sketch map of Sydney area—sampling sites indicated by stars 142 E. This has been intensively studied petrologically by McDougall [1961, 1962], and it is from here that rock sam- ples were collected by him for his K-Ar age de- terminations. The dolerite of the Red Hill area is intrusive into fiat-lying Permian and Triassic sediments (mainly into the Permian beds). The form of the intrusion is essentially that of a dolerite sheet about 400 meters thick, which is gently transgressire upward through the Per- mian sequence from east to west. The Red Hill dike is up to 1500 meters wide and ex- tends almost vertically upward from the un- derlying sheet for over 350 meters. It can be traced north and south of the area studied for a total length of over 10 km. The field rela- tions suggest that the intrusion was initially roofed by sediments. The mean directions of all beds studied of Permian age, except the Upper Tartarian of Russian (Khramov 1961) are positive. The Upper Tartarian, which is sometimes classified with the Triassic by geologists, has both positive and negative or mixed polarities. Negative or mixed polarities characterize Lower Triassic beds elsewhere in the world. Beds laid down in the time range uppermost Carboniferous to uppermost Permian are characterized by having mean directions with positive polarity. This is not statistical; all the formations studied show this feature and Table 5 shows that these give a fair coverage of this span of time, so that although further sampling may reveal negative directions the chances of them being of more than subsidiary importance is considered unlikely. This span of time does not coincide with the geological Permian period and there is, of course, no reason why it should do so. In western Europe the change from negative to positive appears to occur within the West- phalian or between the Westphalian and Stephenian although the actual level has not yet been identified on the ground. Introduction This paper gives an account of field observations and laboratory analysis of the magnetic properties of igneous rock samples collected from the standard Permian sections in Australia. Previous work of a very preliminary nature has been reported by Mercanton (1926) and Irving & Green (1958). The purpose of this study is to attempt to estimate the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field in Permian time in Australia since these igneous rocks may have acquired a thermo- remanent magnetization in the direction of the field at the time of cooling. K-Ar dating, using the whole-rock technique on 20 samples from 12 widely scattered localities, indicates that activ- ity commenced at least 4.5 m.y. ago and that the main period of eruption was in the Late Pliocene and in the Pleistocene. Some of the basalts contain an appreciable amount of glass or finely crystallized material; from consistency of the data it appears that little or no loss of radiogenic Ar has occurred. The specimens dated were mainly obtained from the same localities that Irving and Green had previously sampled for palcomagnetic measurements. Hence the age data provide additional information on geomagnetic polarity epochs and reversals of the earth's magnetic field. Together with previously published results, the new K-Ar dates strongly suggest that a change from normal to reversed polarity occurred 0.75 ñ 0.07 m.y. ago. This polarity change may be the boundary between the Brunhes normal and the Matuyama reversed epochs; alternatively this change may record a short period of reversed polarity (i.e., an event) about 0.81 m.y. ago in an otherwise normal polarity epoch. inclination extends down well into the Upper Carboniferous, so that most of the direction change (aside from reversals and secular variation) occurring between the Upper Silurian and mid-Cretaceous was concentrated in a comparatively short time in the Carboniferous. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: inclination extends down well into the Upper Carboniferous, so that most of the direction change (aside from reversals and secular variation) occurring between the Upper Silurian and mid-Cretaceous was concentrated in a comparatively short time in the Carboniferous. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. inclination extends down well into the Upper Carboniferous, so that most of the direction change (aside from reversals and secular variation) occurring between the Upper Silurian and mid-Cretaceous was concentrated in a comparatively short time in the Carboniferous. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. inclination extends down well into the Upper Carboniferous, so that most of the direction change (aside from reversals and secular variation) occurring between the Upper Silurian and mid-Cretaceous was concentrated in a comparatively short time in the Carboniferous. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. The inclination change corresponds to a lati- tude change of southeastern Australia from about 30øS to about 75øS over a period of prob- ably not more than 20 m.y. This change coincides at its beginning with the Kanimblan orogeny (the largest tectonic event in eastern Australia) and associated marine regression, and is marked at its end by the onset of positive (reversed) polarity which persist to near the end of the Paleozoic in the Australian sections. Direction changes also occurred in Europe at this time, but they were smaller, suggesting that an episode of relative land movement (called the mid-Carboniferous continental drift episode) occurred before the episode invoked by Wegener and others for the late Mesozoic and Cenozoic. These results indicate that there was a correlation in the Upper Carboniferous of a change of latitude and orogeny (and possi- ble drift episode) with a change in reversal frequency, implying a connection between events in the core and at the earth's surface. Moreover, the palaeomagnetic pole calculated from these directions is closer to Tertiary poles from Australia than to the present pole. On this data it is statistically more probable that the NRMs are of Tertiary rather than recent age. Their char­ acteristics are the same as viscous PTRMs, and they are likely to have been acquired during a period of slightly elevated rock temperatures. Most of the results are of measurement of total NRM, but certain samples were selected for alternating field or thermal demagnetization with a view to testing the stability of remanence. Directions of NRM in individual specimens may be represented as unit vectors at a point; the resultant RN of N vectors at a site is a measure of precision. Those site mean directions which are shown to be significant at the 95% confidence level (Watson, 1956) are then repre­ sented by unit vectors in calculating the mean direction of NRM for the group of rocks. The resultant (R) of the site mean vectors is related to the estimate (k) of between-site precision by the equation B --- 1 k = --­ B-R (Fisher, 1953) where B is the number of sites. The palaeomagnetic pole (</>, A) was calculated on the assumption of a geocentric dipole configuration of the geomag­ netic field at the time when rocks were magnetized. 2. The mean direotions of NRM (Table 3) in the granite and its aureole are not significantly different, and have been combined by the conservative procedure of giving unit weight to each site. The results from Cambrian hornfels at sites VI and V2 have been analysed with the Cambrian rocks (Table 1); it is possible that they lie within the aureole of the Housetop Granite, and perhaps should ibe analysed here. However, it will be shown later (Figure 2) that there is no significant difference between directions in Cambrian and Devonian rocks and all will be analysed together (Table 4). 3. CONCLUSIONS. The only suggestion of primary NRM in the rocks described here is from the Eugenana Beds, and this cannot be discussed in detail because the collection was so small. Insufficient outcrop pre­ vents further study, and there is little prospect of confirming the age of NRM in these beds. The NRM in Cambrian sediments and volcanics is considered to be younger than the folding because precision is much greater before than after correction for folding. The agreement between directions before correction in these rocks and those in the Ordovician sandstones and the Devon­ ian granite 'and its aureole-a wide variety of rock types-sugges

from the present field (p = 0,05), its inclination is slightly steeper, and the palaeomagnetic pole position (55W, 68N) is closer to that postulated for Australia during the Lower Tertiary than it is to the present pole-the mean pole calculated by Irving (1964) from several studies of early Tertiary rocks being (50W, 65N). Although the possibility that the NRMs reported here are of recent origin cannot be ruled out, it is more probable that they are of Tertiary age. Evidence for this is strongest for the Cambrian rocks, for which the circular standard error of the mean NRM direction excludes the present field direction. Thermal demagnetization curves of Cambrian tuff from site D3 and hornfels from site D9 (Figures 3 and 4), are characterised by a broad distribution of blocking temperatures, although this is masked to some extent at D9 by the alterations which are introduced by heating above 300°C. NRMs which have been built up over long period of time at slightly elevated tempera­ tures ('viscous PTRMs ') commonly have this same property (Briden, 1965). The jaspilites are thought to have been chemically precipitated in a narrow coastal basin (Miles 1954). Forty-two samples of jaspilite were collected, mainly from surface outcrops. tization results indicate that the bulk of the NRM is carried by grains of low coercivities. The anisotropy of susceptibility of the jaspilites was determined with a low field torque meter (King & Rees 1962). It is clear that the magnetic fabric will be dominated by the textural anisotropy caused by the alternation of silica and iron oxide bands. Thus the axes of minimum susceptibility form a tight group around the normal of the banding plane. Maximum susceptibility axes lie within the banding plane without any preferred orientation within this plane. Lineation and foliation vary considerably from sample to sample but their ratio is fairly constant and about 0.33. The textural anisotropy of the jaspilites is presumably responsible for the low inclinations of the NRM directions with respect to the banding plane. The Iron Monarch ore body forms the largest deposit of the Middleback Ranges. It occurs in a northerly pitching syncline, terminating in the north at the North Wall amphibolite dyke, which is thought to have presented a barrier to the ore forming solutions (Miles 1954). The ore is high-grade hematite, with some admixture of manganese minerals in particular in the north-eastern parts of the body. The ore is generally hard and massive but locally grades into soft earthy hematite. Under reflected light hematite is seen as fine grained (lop-1OOp) interlocking crystals. No specular hematite is observed and magnetite is some- times present as small needle-like inclusions in the hematite crystals. tralia F. H. Chamalaun and H. Porath (Received I967 October 1 I)* Suniinary The results of a palaeomagnetic study on high-grade hematite ore bodies of South Australia are reported. The two major ore bodies, Iron Mon- arch and Iron Prince, gave consistent directions of magnetization with either steep to moderate negative and positive inclinations. The positive and negative groups of hon Monarch are not antiparallel. Because of the presumably long time interval represented by the sampling, this is inter- preted as being due to polar wandering with a superimposed reversal of the Earth’s field. The remanent magnetization is carried by hematite and is extremely stable against alternating field and thermal demagnetiza- tion. The intensity of the NRM is very weak compared to the TRM, which suggests it to be n CRM in origin. Lack of a detailed polar wandering curve for the Pre-Cambrian of Australia prevents precise palaeo- magnetic dating of the ores, but the results clearly suggest a Pre-Cambrian age. In the case of the Middleback Ranges, Miles suggests the fluids to be associated with granitic intrusions. A further problem is the determination of the age of the ores. The Iron Monarch ore body forms the largest deposit of the Middleback Ranges. In the case of the Middleback Ranges, Miles suggests the fluids to be associated with granitic intrusions. A further problem is the determination of the age of the ores. t Summary Iron ore deposits of the Lake Superior type within the Archaean and Proterozoic banded iron formations of Western Australia show consistent and stable directions of remanent magnetization. The palaeomagnetic poles of the ores do not correlate with poles of Post-Cambrian Australian rocks, which suggests a Pre-Cambrian age for the ore formation. Mag- netic anisotropies of the ores are low and the distribution of the principal susceptibility axes tends to reflect the magnetic fabric of the host rocks. 1. Introduction In a previous publication (Chamalaun & Porath 1967) we reported the results of a palaeomagnetic study on the hematite ore bodies of the Middleback Ranges in South Australia. It was found that these were consistently and stably magnetized with a Pre-Cambrian direction. We therefore extended the study to the Western Australian ore bodies, the results of which are reported here. A large number of high-grade hematite ore bodies are known to occur in the Archaean and Proterozoic banded iron formations of Western Australia, but in order to obtain fresh subsurface samples we have sampled only those that are actively mined. The localities of the ore bodies sampled are shown in Fig. 1. The Mt Goldsworthy and Koolyanobbing deposits occur in Archaean banded ir

oterozoic banded iron formations of Western Australia, but in order to obtain fresh subsurface samples we have sampled only those that are actively mined. The localities of the ore bodies sampled are shown in Fig. 1. The Mt Goldsworthy and Koolyanobbing deposits occur in Archaean banded iron forma- tions, whilst the host rocks for the Mt Tom Price and Mt Newman ore bodies are Proterozoic iron formations. 2. Results (a) Mt Goldsworthy. The Mt Goldsworthy deposit is located at the northern extremity of the Western Australian Archaean shield. A folded and faulted banded iron formation, which consists of alternating layers of silica and hematite, forms the host rock of a number of high-grade hematite ore bodies of varying origins. Introduction In a previous publication (Chamalaun & Porath 1967) we reported the results of a palaeomagnetic study on the hematite ore bodies of the Middleback Ranges in South Australia. To compare the land-based polar changes with the ocean-floor drift south of Australia requires that a series of poles from well-dated rocks be determined with considerable accuracy (polar errors of 5" or less). Previous palaeomagnetic measurements are generally inadequate for this purpose, either because the age of the rocks was not known precisely or because large polar errors resulted from sampling at only a few localities. Twenty sites in the Older Volcanics of Victoria have been studies by Mumme (1963) following a preliminary investigation by Green & Irving (1958). On palaeonto- logical grounds these basalts are thought to be Palaeoceilto Eocene in age (Cookson & Dettman 1959; Singleton & Joyce 1969). Irving, Stott &Ward (1961) investigated eight sites from the Tertiary basalts of.New South Wales. The localities sampled are now known to range in age from about 15 to 45 m.yr (McDougall & Wilkinson 1967; Stipp & McDougall 1968; and other unpublished information). Volcanics in southern Queensland have been studied at 11 sites by Robertson (1966). Webb, Stevens & McDougall (1967) report the age of these rocks as ranging from 25 to 21 m.yr. The Newer Volcanics of Victoria have been investigated by Green & Irving (1958), Parry (1960) and McDo

(1966). These latter authors found their K-Ar age ranged from 5 to 05m.yr, and other evidence indicates activity until about 5000 years ago.
